description: I’m a CSE student at Gopalganj Science and Technology University (GSTU), passionate about programming, technology, problem-solving, and space exploration. I enjoy building creative web and educational projects. For NASA Space Apps, I’m looking for teammates interested in programming, data analysis, astronomy, research, and presentation. Curiosity, teamwork, and creativity matter most. 🚀🌌
summary:
We created Space Legacy, a web storybook for children ages 8 to 14. It uses NASA’s data and images to let kids explore the solar system. They can open a profile. Read a first-person letter for each space machine. They follow a timeline check a "Where are they now" page try out science explainers and earn badges and a certificate by answering quizzes.

The storybook answers a challenge: most space stories stop at launch day. Kids rarely learn what the machines actually discovered or why they still help missions like Artemis. Space Legacy tells the stories of NASA’s equipment on the Moon on Mars and in space. It includes Apollo hardware, the Opportunity rover, the InSight lander and the Voyager spacecraft.

It keeps the voice separate, from verified NASA facts. It explains the science each machine made possible. This matters because kids need to see the journey, not just the beginning. Space Legacy turns real NASA data into learning that's easy to understand. It builds curiosity. Inspires the next generation of explorers.
details:
Space Legacy is an interactive web storybook that tells the stories of the machines NASA has left on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space. It is built for school-age space enthusiasts (ages 8 to 14). Kids explore a map of the solar system and tap a machine to open its profile: its mission, its discoveries, how its mission ended, and why it matters today. Each machine also has a first-person letter, such as Opportunity telling kids it was built to last 90 days and lasted nearly fifteen years, kept clearly separate from verified NASA facts. A timeline, a Where are they now page that estimates the distance and signal time of Voyager and Pioneer from dated NASA reference values, and science explainers (dust storms and solar panels, marsquakes, and the Moon’s laser reflectors) turn each story into hands-on learning. Quizzes earn badges and a printable certificate, and signed-in explorers save their progress and favorites. Mission facts come from NASA’s public pages and are stored in structured content files that the site reads.

Benefits: children learn real science from real missions in a friendly, story-driven way. The site works on phones, in light and dark themes, with glossary tooltips for technical words, keyboard navigation, and text-size and reduced-motion options.

Intended impact: we want children to see old equipment as the beginning of discovery, not as junk in space, and to connect past machines to future missions like Artemis. As it grows, Space Legacy can add more machines, more languages, and classroom use so more children can meet these stories.

Tools: TypeScript, React, TanStack Start, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Framer Motion, with a cloud backend for sign-in and saved progress. Data and images come from NASA Science, NASA History, NASA JPL, and the NASA Image and Video Library, credited on the site. We used Claude for planning, writing, and debugging help, and Antigravity as a coding assistant. Our team checked all facts against NASA’s pages and reviewed and tested all code and content.

Creativity: instead of presenting data, we let each machine speak in its own voice, turned the solar system into a museum with no roof, and made science playful, for example by sliding a dust storm to watch a rover’s battery drain.

Factors we considered: accuracy first (every fact comes from NASA, and changing numbers are shown as dated estimates), a child-friendly reading level, accessibility, privacy (we save only a name, avatar, and progress), fast loading on phones, crediting every source and image, and being open about our use of AI.
